n: News of the Jordan miracle spreads to the kings west of the river and along the coast. Their courage melts — giving Israel a window of safety to renew its covenant.
God commands that the men be circumcised — a “second time” for the nation, renewing the covenant sign the wilderness generation had neglected.

f.g: Literally “knives of flint” — stone blades used for sacred rites.

n: Joshua carries out the command at a site nicknamed “the hill of the foreskins.”
The reason: the men who left Egypt had all died during the forty years.
Those who left Egypt were circumcised, but sons born in the wilderness had not been.

f.g: Possibly because of the people’s rebellion and the hardships of travel.

n: Forty years of wandering came because the Exodus generation disobeyed; God swore they would not see the land.

f.w: because they obeyed not the voice of the LORD

n: Their children, raised up in their place, received the covenant sign under Joshua. A new generation makes its own covenant.

f.w: whom he raised up in their stead

n: The men stayed in camp until they healed — a vulnerable moment that required trust in God’s protection, right on the enemy’s doorstep.
God says he has “rolled away” the shame of Egypt. The name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew word for “roll.” Their slave identity was gone; they were a covenant people.

f.w: I rolled away the reproach of Egypt

n: Israel keeps its first Passover in the promised land, on the 14th day of the first month at evening — forty years after the first one in Egypt.
The next day they ate produce of the land — unleavened bread and roasted grain — fulfilling God’s promise of a land of plenty.

f.g: Stored grain or produce of the land.

n: The manna stopped the day after. God’s miraculous provision ends when ordinary means become available — he doesn’t do for us what we can now do ourselves.
Near Jericho, Joshua sees a man with a drawn sword and boldly asks, “Are you with us or against us?”

f.w: his sword drawn in his hand

n: “Neither” — he is the commander of the Lord’s army. The real question isn’t whether God is on our side, but whether we are on his. Joshua bows in worship.

f.w: captain of the host of the LORD
f.g: Commander of the Lord’s army (of angels).
Bowed down; he accepts the worship, suggesting a divine messenger.

n: As with Moses at the burning bush, Joshua must remove his sandals on holy ground. Joshua is confirmed as Moses’ successor in sacred experience too.

f.w: Loose thy shoe from off thy foot
